https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6706/3502533/ Extinct glitch classes living fossils tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk O and O Light Modulation Status Known from Hanford during O and O Doubtful very rare if present from Livingston during O Not seen during O or O so far believed extinct This is a glitch class which has been named for the subsystem in which the cause had resided but described and defined by its visual appearance It turns out that other kinds of malfunctions in the same subsystem later caused quite a variety of glitches that look totally different some that were given other names some remaining nameless There exist glitches coming from the laser light modulation machinery which do not at all resemble the Light Modulation class for which the Gravity Spy Machine Learning has been trained and which is described in our Field Guide Conversely glitch shapes which somewhat resemble the original Light Modulation glitches compound shapes which look like a blip followed by low frequency noise can arise in other ways from causes that have nothing to do with the light modulation machinery False friends As a results hundreds of O subjects and at least dozens of O subjects have got mis labeled as Light Modulation by the ML Background The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where something could sometimes go wrong all of which would need to be investigated by the LIGO engineers during glitch hunting There's a reference oscillator running at MHz LHO tab ! LHO EOM in its surroundings ! LHO EOM connections Some of the equipment including some of the RF cables in the electronics room just to give an impression ! LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! "None Of The Above" is always an option when something doesn't seem to fit into the available classes and it ensures that more people are going to get a look The "Repeating Blips" class available from the level workflow onwards was originally introduced to capture rows of blips that are all more or less the same size and shape and occupy the same frequency range where some cause was at work repeatedly up to several times per second and each time it happened it produced one single blip It could also happen that two blips of similar or different sizes and shapes appear together in the same subject image by mere coincidence But after "Repeating Blips" had been introduced we've also encountered other groups of multiple blips of which the present subject is a good example where a few blip like glitches of different sizes appear in a fairly tight group with irregular spacing along the time axis and with a definite beginning and end within the four seconds we get to see These have got nicknamed "flocks" and they appear to be a genuine seeparate glitch class of their own which has yet to be formally proposed Here it appears that a single cause is at work just once but couples into the gravitational strain channel through two or three distinct causal connections producing the entire group when it happens There's some prior discussion of these g here tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk If you see more of these why not start a collection of them? First of all it doesn't contain valid data near Hz where the loud glitch in strain appears tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2961842?comment so there's no way it could directly witness this glitch up there The same applies to H ASC REFL B RF Q YAW OUT DQ and H LSC POP A LF OUT DQ in tab and tab Second it does however have some noise at lower frequencies which starts and ends at the right moments Third there's loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz surrounded by spikes which suddenly stops around the time of the glitch and a dark whitening artefact band afterwards Fourth there's less loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz which suddenly starts around the time of the glitch and a dark artefact band at this frequency before this point So what could possibly show up at a fairly high frequency in the strain channel on the output side of the interferometer and in a REFL channel on the input side even before the Power Recycling Cavity !? Noting that the PRC length could not easily produce fluctuations this fast in the arm cavities and that the alignment sensing and control loops are far slower Which leaves laser frequency noise that's normally controlled by a fast multi level feedback loop acting back on the PreStabilized Laser and locking it against the common arm length CARM so as to keep CARM at a constant multiple of the instantaneous laser wavelength And these glitches only happened between and Armed with this knowledge we head to the LHO logbook and find LHO tab The Hanford team aiming to improve noise levels at frequencies of several kHz had been experimenting from onwards with a higher gain of the CARM feedback loop On this change was reverted upon noticing that it had not helped as intended and that it had resulted in worse noise levels at some frequencies during the first two hours of each lock while the optics were gradually approaching thermal equilibrium It was also noticed that at this higher gain setting after each lock reacquisition some 1h 40m actually between one hour and two hours after reaching Nominal Low Noise and independently of when Observing resumed something changed state quite rapidly causing noise components near and kHz to disappear and noise near kHz to appear instead It turns out that our glitches happened during these state changes and that within each lock segment several of them could happen in succession before the changed state settled down All fourty five known glitches of this kind happened between one hour and two hours after reaching NLN from comparing the approximate timestamps to which we currently have access to the Detector Status Summary Pages from tab It also becomes clear why none of these glitches happened on because LHO kept observing and didn't lose lock until the evening and didn't resume Observing allowing glitches to be recorded after a UTC lock reacquisition until UTC the next day this time more than two hours after reaching NLN baffle that was vibrating at a rate of several times per second modulated by slower pendulum motions one half period every couple of seconds of one of the test mass suspensions These glitches don't happen any more during the ongoing fourth observing run These cryopump baffles which had been vibration prone back then are better damped now The old glitch class proposal thread tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk includes a history of the mitigation efforts with links to some logbook entries with pictures The auxiliary channel represents the small amount of laser light that gets through the reflective mirror coating of Livingston's X end test mass and is picked up by a quadrant photodiode used in Alignment Sensing and Control ASC part of the machinery that keeps the beam spots in their proper places on all four test masses It's quite possible that the Crown glitches came from the Y end Since micro seismic ground motion happens at its own pace at each of the corner station and the two end stations several km away the motions of the test mass suspensions or better the motions of the vacuum chambers around each test mass and everything attached to the chamber walls are independent Seismic activity may be elevated in all three locations but any resulting glitches could well be interleaved like they are here The Glitch Paleontological Museum Over the last nine years writing in late Advanced LIGO has come a long way The interferometers and the glitch mix coming out of them! have changed faster than the Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the subject didn't in fact fit anywhere among the classes known to the ML Combining the data release tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2583278?comment with a deep dive into old logbook entries yields some insights and a few surprises to me at any rate Shovels ready? Prepared to get your fingers dirty? https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6706/3502533/ Extinct glitch classes living fossils tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk O and O Light Modulation Status Known from Hanford during O and O Doubtful very rare if present from Livingston during O Not seen during O or O so far believed extinct This is a glitch class which has been named for the subsystem in which the cause had resided but described and defined by its visual appearance It turns out that other kinds of malfunctions in the same subsystem later caused quite a variety of glitches that look totally different some that were given other names some remaining nameless There exist glitches coming from the laser light modulation machinery which do not at all resemble the Light Modulation class for which the Gravity Spy Machine Learning has been trained and which is described in our Field Guide Conversely glitch shapes which somewhat resemble the original Light Modulation glitches compound shapes which look like a blip followed by low frequency noise can arise in other ways from causes that have nothing to do with the light modulation machinery False friends As a results hundreds of O subjects and at least dozens of O subjects have got mis labeled as Light Modulation by the ML Background The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where something could sometimes go wrong all of which would need to be investigated by the LIGO      Interesting catch! Well obviously it did happen more examples of this kind will be welcome This is part of a subject set of glitches from Livingston that happened during the first months of the third observing run the present subject dates from the second day of O3a which had been processed and uploaded for use in Gravity Spy a year and a half ago but which have only now been associated with the active workflows So this is the very first example of its kind that we're getting to see The glitch in strain is a Crown a fast scattering glitch where the stray light was reflected by the edge of a large cylindrical baffle that was vibrating at a rate of several times per second modulated by slower pendulum motions one half period every couple of seconds of one of the test mass suspensions These glitches don't happen any more during the ongoing fourth observing run These cryopump baffles which had been vibration prone back then are better damped now The old glitch class proposal thread tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk includes a history of the mitigation efforts with links to some logbook entries with pictures The auxiliary channel represents the small amount of laser light that gets through the reflective mirror coating of Livingston's X end test mass and is picked up by a quadrant photodiode used in Alignment Sensing and Control ASC part of the machinery that keeps the beam spots in their proper places on all four test masses It's quite possible that the Crown glitches came from the Y end Since micro seismic ground motion happens at its own pace at each of the corner station and the two end stations several km away the motions of the test mass suspensions or better the motions of the vacuum chambers around each test mass and everything attached to the chamber walls are independent Seismic activity may be elevated in all three locations but any resulting glitches could well be interleaved like they are here LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! "None Of The Above" is always an option when something doesn't seem to fit into the available classes and it ensures that more people are going to get a look The "Repeating Blips" class available from the level workflow onwards was originally introduced to capture rows of blips that are all more or less the same size and shape and occupy the same frequency range where some cause was at work repeatedly up to several times per second and each time it happened it produced one single blip It could also happen that two blips of similar or different sizes and shapes appear together in the same subject image by mere coincidence But after "Repeating Blips" had been introduced we've also encountered other groups of multiple blips of which the present subject is a good example where a few blip like glitches of different sizes appear in a fairly tight group with irregular spacing along the time axis and with a definite beginning and end within the four seconds we get to see These have got nicknamed "flocks" and they appear to be a genuine seeparate glitch class of their own which has yet to be formally proposed Here it appears that a single cause is at work just once but couples into the gravitational strain channel through two or three distinct causal connections producing the entire group when it happens There's some prior discussion of these g here tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk If you see more of these why not start a collection of them? First of all it doesn't contain valid data near Hz where the loud glitch in strain appears tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2961842?comment so there's no way it could directly witness this glitch up there The same applies to H ASC REFL B RF Q YAW OUT DQ and H LSC POP A LF OUT DQ in tab and tab Second it does however have some noise at lower frequencies which starts and ends at the right moments Third there's loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz surrounded by spikes which suddenly stops around the time of the glitch and a dark whitening artefact band afterwards Fourth there's less loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz which suddenly starts around the time of the glitch and a dark artefact band at this frequency before this point So what could possibly show up at a fairly high frequency in the strain channel on the output side of the interferometer and in a REFL channel on the input side even before the Power Recycling Cavity !? Noting that the PRC length could not easily produce fluctuations this fast in the arm cavities and that the alignment sensing and control loops are far slower Which leaves laser frequency noise that's normally controlled by a fast multi level feedback loop acting back on the PreStabilized Laser and locking it against the common arm length CARM so as to keep CARM at a constant multiple of the instantaneous laser wavelength And these glitches only happened between and Armed with this knowledge we head to the LHO logbook and find LHO tab The Hanford team aiming to improve noise levels at frequencies of several kHz had been experimenting from onwards with a higher gain of the CARM feedback loop On this change was reverted upon noticing that it had not helped as intended and that it had resulted in worse noise levels at some frequencies during the first two hours of each lock while the optics were gradually approaching thermal equilibrium It was also noticed that at this higher gain setting after each lock reacquisition some 1h 40m actually between one hour and two hours after reaching Nominal Low Noise and independently of when Observing resumed something changed state quite rapidly causing noise components near and kHz to disappear and noise near kHz to appear instead It turns out that our glitches happened during these state changes and that within each lock segment several of them could happen in succession before the changed state settled down All fourty five known glitches of this kind happened between one hour and two hours after reaching NLN from comparing the approximate timestamps to which we currently have access to the Detector Status Summary Pages from tab It also becomes clear why none of these glitches happened on because LHO kept observing and didn't lose lock until the evening and didn't resume Observing allowing glitches to be recorded after a UTC lock reacquisition until UTC the next day this time more than two hours after reaching NLN The Glitch Paleontological Museum Over the last nine years writing in late Advanced LIGO has come a long way The interferometers and the glitch mix coming out of them! have changed faster than the Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the subject didn't in fact fit anywhere among the classes known to the ML Combining the data release tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2583278?comment with a deep dive into old logbook entries yields some insights and a few surprises to me at any rate Shovels ready? Prepared to get your fingers dirty? https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6706/3502533/ Extinct glitch classes living fossils tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk O and O Light Modulation Status Known from Hanford during O and O Doubtful very rare if present from Livingston during O Not seen during O or O so far believed extinct This is a glitch class which has been named for the subsystem in which the cause had resided but described and defined by its visual appearance It turns out that other kinds of malfunctions in the same subsystem later caused quite a variety of glitches that look totally different some that were given other names some remaining nameless There exist glitches coming from the laser light modulation machinery which do not at all resemble the Light Modulation class for which the Gravity Spy Machine Learning has been trained and which is described in our Field Guide Conversely glitch shapes which somewhat resemble the original Light Modulation glitches compound shapes which look like a blip followed by low frequency noise can arise in other ways from causes that have nothing to do with the light modulation machinery False friends As a results hundreds of O subjects and at least dozens of O subjects have got mis labeled as Light Modulation by the ML Background The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where something could sometimes go wrong all of which would need to be investigated by the LIGO engineers during glitch hunting There's a reference oscillator running at MHz LHO tab ! LHO EOM in its surroundings ! LHO EOM connections Some of the equipment including some of the RF cables in the electronics room just to give an impression ! LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! "None Of The Above" is always an option when something doesn't seem to fit into the available classes and it ensures that more people are going to get a look The "Repeating Blips" class available from the level workflow onwards was originally introduced to capture rows of blips that are all more or less the same size and shape and occupy the same frequency range where some cause was at work repeatedly up to several times per second and each time it happened it produced one single blip It could also happen that two blips of similar or different sizes and shapes appear together in the same subject image by mere coincidence But after "Repeating Blips" had been introduced we've also encountered other groups of multiple blips of which the present subject is a good example where a few blip like glitches of different sizes appear in a fairly tight group with irregular spacing along the time axis and with a definite beginning and end within the four seconds we get to see These have got nicknamed "flocks" and they appear to be a genuine seeparate glitch class of their own which has yet to be formally proposed Here it appears that a single cause is at work just once but couples into the gravitational strain channel through two or three distinct causal connections producing the entire group when it happens There's some prior discussion of these g here tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk If you see more of these why not start a collection of them? First of all it doesn't contain valid data near Hz where the loud glitch in strain appears tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2961842?comment so there's no way it could directly witness this glitch up there The same applies to H ASC REFL B RF Q YAW OUT DQ and H LSC POP A LF OUT DQ in tab and tab Second it does however have some noise at lower frequencies which starts and ends at the right moments Third there's loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz surrounded by spikes which suddenly stops around the time of the glitch and a dark whitening artefact band afterwards Fourth there's less loud narrowband noise somewhere around Hz which suddenly starts around the time of the glitch and a dark artefact band at this frequency before this point So what could possibly show up at a fairly high frequency in the strain channel on the output side of the interferometer and in a REFL channel on the input side even before the Power Recycling Cavity !? Noting that the PRC length could not easily produce fluctuations this fast in the arm cavities and that the alignment sensing and control loops are far slower Which leaves laser frequency noise that's normally controlled by a fast multi level feedback loop acting back on the PreStabilized Laser and locking it against the common arm length CARM so as to keep CARM at a constant multiple of the instantaneous laser wavelength And these glitches only happened between and Armed with this knowledge we head to the LHO logbook and find LHO tab The Hanford team aiming to improve noise levels at frequencies of several kHz had been experimenting from onwards with a higher gain of the CARM feedback loop On this change was reverted upon noticing that it had not helped as intended and that it had resulted in worse noise levels at some frequencies during the first two hours of each lock while the optics were gradually approaching thermal equilibrium It was also noticed that at this higher gain setting after each lock reacquisition some 1h 40m actually between one hour and two hours after reaching Nominal Low Noise and independently of when Observing resumed something changed state quite rapidly causing noise components near and kHz to disappear and noise near kHz to appear instead It turns out that our glitches happened during these state changes and that within each lock segment several of them could happen in succession before the changed state settled down All fourty five known glitches of this kind happened between one hour and two hours after reaching NLN from comparing the approximate timestamps to which we currently have access to the Detector Status Summary Pages from tab It also becomes clear why none of these glitches happened on because LHO kept observing and didn't lose lock until the evening and didn't resume Observing allowing glitches to be recorded after a UTC lock reacquisition until UTC the next day this time more than two hours after reaching NLN baffle that was vibrating at a rate of several times per second modulated by slower pendulum motions one half period every couple of seconds of one of the test mass suspensions These glitches don't happen any more during the ongoing fourth observing run These cryopump baffles which had been vibration prone back then are better damped now The old glitch class proposal thread tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk includes a history of the mitigation efforts with links to some logbook entries with pictures The auxiliary channel represents the small amount of laser light that gets through the reflective mirror coating of Livingston's X end test mass and is picked up by a quadrant photodiode used in Alignment Sensing and Control ASC part of the machinery that keeps the beam spots in their proper places on all four test masses It's quite possible that the Crown glitches came from the Y end Since micro seismic ground motion happens at its own pace at each of the corner station and the two end stations several km away the motions of the test mass suspensions or better the motions of the vacuum chambers around each test mass and everything attached to the chamber walls are independent Seismic activity may be elevated in all three locations but any resulting glitches could well be interleaved like they are here The Glitch Paleontological Museum Over the last nine years writing in late Advanced LIGO has come a long way The interferometers and the glitch mix coming out of them! have changed faster than the Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the subject didn't in fact fit anywhere among the classes known to the ML Combining the data release tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2583278?comment with a deep dive into old logbook entries yields some insights and a few surprises to me at any rate Shovels ready? Prepared to get your fingers dirty? https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/6706/3502533/ Extinct glitch classes living fossils tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk O and O Light Modulation Status Known from Hanford during O and O Doubtful very rare if present from Livingston during O Not seen during O or O so far believed extinct This is a glitch class which has been named for the subsystem in which the cause had resided but described and defined by its visual appearance It turns out that other kinds of malfunctions in the same subsystem later caused quite a variety of glitches that look totally different some that were given other names some remaining nameless There exist glitches coming from the laser light modulation machinery which do not at all resemble the Light Modulation class for which the Gravity Spy Machine Learning has been trained and which is described in our Field Guide Conversely glitch shapes which somewhat resemble the original Light Modulation glitches compound shapes which look like a blip followed by low frequency noise can arise in other ways from causes that have nothing to do with the light modulation machinery False friends As a results hundreds of O subjects and at least dozens of O subjects have got mis labeled as Light Modulation by the ML Background The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where something could sometimes go wrong all of which would need to be investigated by the LIGO      Interesting catch! Well obviously it did happen more examples of this kind will be welcome This is part of a subject set of glitches from Livingston that happened during the first months of the third observing run the present subject dates from the second day of O3a which had been processed and uploaded for use in Gravity Spy a year and a half ago but which have only now been associated with the active workflows So this is the very first example of its kind that we're getting to see The glitch in strain is a Crown a fast scattering glitch where the stray light was reflected by the edge of a large cylindrical baffle that was vibrating at a rate of several times per second modulated by slower pendulum motions one half period every couple of seconds of one of the test mass suspensions These glitches don't happen any more during the ongoing fourth observing run These cryopump baffles which had been vibration prone back then are better damped now The old glitch class proposal thread tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk includes a history of the mitigation efforts with links to some logbook entries with pictures The auxiliary channel represents the small amount of laser light that gets through the reflective mirror coating of Livingston's X end test mass and is picked up by a quadrant photodiode used in Alignment Sensing and Control ASC part of the machinery that keeps the beam spots in their proper places on all four test masses It's quite possible that the Crown glitches came from the Y end Since micro seismic ground motion happens at its own pace at each of the corner station and the two end stations several km away the motions of the test mass suspensions or better the motions of the vacuum chambers around each test mass and everything attached to the chamber walls are independent Seismic activity may be elevated in all three locations but any resulting glitches could well be interleaved like they are here The Glitch Paleontological Museum Over the last nine years writing in late Advanced LIGO has come a long way The interferometers and the glitch mix coming out of them! have changed faster than the Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the subject didn't in fact fit anywhere among the classes known to the ML Combining the data release tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2583278?comment with a deep dive into old logbook entries      Interesting catch! Well obviously it did happen more examples of this kind will be welcome This is part of a subject set of glitches from Livingston that happened during the first months of the third observing run the present subject dates from the second day of O3a which had been processed and uploaded for use in Gravity Spy a year and a half ago but which have only now been associated with the active workflows So this is the very first example of its kind that we're getting to see The glitch in strain is a Crown a fast scattering glitch where the stray light was reflected by the edge of a large cylindrical baffle that was vibrating at a rate of several times per second modulated by slower pendulum motions one half period every couple of seconds of one of the test mass suspensions These glitches don't happen any more during the ongoing fourth observing run These cryopump baffles which had been vibration prone back then are better damped now The old glitch class proposal thread tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk includes a history of the mitigation efforts with links to some logbook entries with pictures The auxiliary channel represents the small amount of laser light that gets through the reflective mirror coating of Livingston's X end test mass and is picked up by a quadrant photodiode used in Alignment Sensing and Control ASC part of the machinery that keeps the beam spots in their proper places on all four test masses It's quite possible that the Crown glitches came from the Y end Since micro seismic ground motion happens at its own pace at each of the corner station and the two end stations several km away the motions of the test mass suspensions or better the motions of the vacuum chambers around each test mass and everything attached to the chamber walls are independent Seismic activity may be elevated in all three locations but any resulting glitches could well be interleaved like they are here The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=74155 Jorge Stuart H Stuart A TJ many others both on and off site SHORT VERSION The BBSS used to drift We have found a BBSS configuration that doesn't drift after some extended settling time However the BBSS configuration that doesn't drift has extreme blade positions so we hope to change d and d parameters to get a more "healthy" BBSS We have been fighting a pitch drift in the BBSS for some time Here is what we know The pitch drift is not a thermal effect and is seen always in one direction The daily drift due to temperature can sometimes be seen on top of the pitch drift but the drift dominates The drift is usually pretty linear over long periods of time The drift is primarily in the top mass M and M stages see far less of the drift but do move slowly as the top mass moves Since the drift is dominated by M we have tried a lot of different configurations Initially we thought the blades that hold the wire leading from M to M was to high this is related to the d parameter of a suspension So we lowered the blades and tried a couple different configurations Then it was discovered that the issue was not from the blades on M but rather the point where M is supported The "pickup" point of M was below the center of mass while nominally it should be above this is the d parameter of a suspension To remedy this we lowered the center of mass on M and lowered the blades on M to ensure that the pickup point of m is above the center of mass and the blade tips leading to M are below the center of mass Initially we were worried that the suspension was still drifting but after a few days and relieving some rubbing the pitch drift was gone Currently we lowered the center of mass further to see if our theory on why the pitch drift stopped is correct but the suspension hasn't had enough time to settle yet The blades are currently quite low mm below there nominal values At some point we hope to raise them to a more reasonable height off nominal To help raise the blades and buy both us an Hanford some margin of stability Betsy is getting some parts fabricated to raise the d value of the suspension Attached is a long drift log with a short description of the many configurations and plots of their pitch F F F are the three bosems that contribute to pitch DAMP P INMON should be calibrated to microradians SUS Gravity Spy glitch class notions Updating the Gravity Spy Machine Learning to accommodate new glitch classes is hard and tedious work tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3369772?comment Some glitch classes from earlier observing runs have gone the way of the trilobites they're well and truly extinct now We've been keeping them around for didactic purposes Some have gone the way of the dinoasaurs their descendants are still among us but they look very different nowadays and no longer resemble their fossil ancestors very much so we now call them "birds" bird Some have gone the way of the Coealacanths They were thought to have gone extinct but seem to have returned tab Or else an entirely different glitch cause may now be at work originating from some component that didn't even exist yet during past observing runs producing false friends lookalike glitches that have re occupied a vacant ecological niche Or a surviving old population of glitches may now be sharing its habitat with a new one of different origin but looking confusingly similar There are fish in the oceans and then there are dolphins too Lookalikes can confuse the Machine Learning and us human volunteers alike In both cases the result is mission creep New phenomena get mistakenly subsumed under old glitch classes where they don't belong Our human brains tend to be biased towards the familiar it takes more of a mental effort to identify something as an unfamiliar "None Of The Above" than to shoehorn it into a known class even though it doesn't belong And the Machine Learning nowadays doesn't even have a way of signalling "None Of The Above" it will label each and every subjects with one of the glitch classes it has been trained for A low estimated confidence would be the only hint that the O or O so far believed extinct This is a glitch class which has been named for the subsystem in which the cause had resided but described and defined by its visual appearance It turns out that other kinds of malfunctions in the same subsystem later caused quite a variety of glitches that look totally different some that were given other names some remaining nameless There exist glitches coming from the laser light modulation machinery which do not at all resemble the Light Modulation class for which the Gravity Spy Machine Learning has been trained and which is described in our Field Guide Conversely glitch shapes which somewhat resemble the original Light Modulation glitches compound shapes which look like a blip followed by low frequency noise can arise in other ways from causes that have nothing to do with the light modulation machinery False friends As a results hundreds of O subjects and at least dozens of O subjects have got mis labeled as Light Modulation by the ML Background The main near infrared nm laser beam gets phase modulated with several short wave radio frequencies including MHz and MHz often abbreviated "RF9" and "RF45" in order to create sidebands some amount of laser light of very slightly shorter and longer wavelengths which unlike the carrier light won't resonate between the test mass mirrors in the arms The sidebands confined to the central interferometer can then be used as a reference against which we can measure tab There are quite a few components involved in creating and applying the radio frequency signals and thus quite a few places where something could sometimes go wrong all of which would need to be investigated by the LIGO engineers during glitch hunting There's a reference oscillator running at MHz LHO tab ! LHO EOM in its surroundings ! LHO EOM connections Some of the equipment including some of the RF cables in the electronics room just to give an impression ! LLO Images from the LIGO logbooks courtesy Caltech MIT LIGO Laboratory tab A brief disturbance of the RF modulation amplitude would show up after demodulation as a spike in several photodiode channels The Length Sensing and Control LSC subsystem might mistake it for a disturbance in the distance between a pair of mirrors and would react by sending signals to the mirror suspensions to "correct" the perceived excursion only to introduce an excursion which then needs to be counteracted during the following tens of milliseconds Similarly the Alignment Sensing and Control ASC subystem might misinterpret such a spike as a mirror or two having turned away from their correct angles and would send a "correction" to the suspensions which afterwards would need to be countermanded These coupling paths are what can give rise to a compound glitch shape in our Gravity Spy images a very brief broadband blip followed by low frequency rumbles during the momentary length and alignment excursions The LSC and ASC control loops have been reworked and refined many times over the years their reactions nowadays would be more subtle The initial blip would often also show up in an auxiliary channel dedicated to monitoring the RF modulation amplitude LSC MOD RF AM CTRL OUT DQ Other kinds of RF malfunctions giving rise to other glitch shapes in our image would also stand a good chance of being witnessed by this channel The original series Hanford September Already during Engineering Run before the first Observing Run of Advanced LIGO there had been occurrences of this kind of glitch and some effort had been made to locate the cause A few days into O from Sunday onwards another spate of these glitches began to plague the Hanford interferometer The linked subject above was among the earliest of these Showing the third frames of some examples ! It turns out that when the Gravity Spy Machine Learning was trained on genuine examples it settled on the shapes of the individual glitchlets without any regard to their periodicity and alternation on their "Dove" aspect without regard to the "Paired" trait Thousands of later glitches of unrelated types have thus ended up with inappropriate Paired Doves labels Background LHO tab Paired Doves glitches were happening while a number of mirrors on the output side of the interferometer were developing oscillations in pitch tipping up and down around a horizontal axis that started gently and gradually got worse over the course of a few minutes each time ending in a lockloss The ultimate cause was never conclusively determined it could have been an instability in the angular control of the Beam Splitter at Hz close to a mechanical resonance of the BS suspension or the BS angular control could itself have been reacting to something else Every actively controlled mirror "downstream" from the BS along the output path was tipping at the same pace trying to track the faint output beam through its vertical wobbles Once the motion had got large enough a glitchlet "dove" appeared whenever the wobbling beam was at the highest or at the lowest point of its excursions Here is a view of Hanford's central Beam Splitter as it looked prior to O from LHO tab ! the like at a range of frequencies coupling into the strain channel at different locations Their appearance in subject images their durations and any periodicities could vary widely and it is a wide out in Aside from general Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning HVAC LIGO uses compressors for two kinds of pressurized air supplies Clean ultra dry purge air at modest pressure above ambient for clean lab rooms temporary clean rooms erected in the experiment halls and venting of vacuum chambers when required and higher pressure instrument air g for operating the large pneumatic gate valves https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=74155 Jorge Stuart H Stuart A TJ many others both on and off site SHORT VERSION The BBSS used to drift We have found a BBSS configuration that doesn't drift after some extended settling time However the BBSS configuration that doesn't drift has extreme blade positions so we hope to change d and d parameters to get a more "healthy" BBSS We have been fighting a pitch drift in the BBSS for some time Here is what we know The pitch drift is not a thermal effect and is seen always in one direction The daily drift due to temperature can sometimes be seen on top of the pitch drift but the drift dominates The drift is usually pretty linear over long periods of time The drift is primarily in the top mass M and M stages see far less of the drift but do move slowly as the top mass moves Since the drift is dominated by M we have tried a lot of different configurations Initially we thought the blades that hold the wire leading from M to M was to high this is related to the d parameter of a suspension So we lowered the blades and tried a couple different configurations Then it was discovered that the issue was not from the blades on M but rather the point where M is supported The "pickup" point of M was below the center of mass while nominally it should be above this is the d parameter of a suspension To remedy this we lowered the center of mass on M and lowered the blades on M to ensure that the pickup point of m is above the center of mass and the blade tips leading to M are below the center of mass Initially we were worried that the suspension was still drifting but after a few days and relieving some rubbing the pitch drift was gone Currently we lowered the center of mass further to see if our theory on why the pitch drift stopped is correct but the suspension hasn't had enough time to settle yet The blades are currently quite low mm below there nominal values At some point we hope to raise them to a more reasonable height off nominal To help raise the blades and buy both us an Hanford some margin of stability Betsy is getting some parts fabricated to raise the d value of the suspension Attached is a long drift log with a short description of the many configurations and plots of their pitch F F F are the three bosems that contribute to pitch DAMP P INMON should be calibrated to microradians SUS https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=74155 Jorge Stuart H Stuart A TJ many others both on and off site SHORT VERSION The BBSS used to drift We have found a BBSS configuration that doesn't drift after some extended settling time However the BBSS configuration that doesn't drift has extreme blade positions so we hope to change d and d parameters to get a more "healthy" BBSS We have been fighting a pitch drift in the BBSS for some time Here is what we know The pitch drift is not a thermal effect and is seen always in one direction The daily drift due to temperature can sometimes be seen on top of the pitch drift but the drift dominates The drift is usually pretty linear over long periods of time The drift is primarily in the top mass M and M stages see far less of the drift but do move slowly as the top mass moves Since the drift is dominated by M we have tried a lot of different configurations Initially we thought the blades that hold the wire leading from M to M was to high this is related to the d parameter of a suspension So we lowered the blades and tried a couple different configurations Then it was discovered that the issue was not from the blades on M but rather the point where M is supported The "pickup" point of M was below the center of mass while nominally it should be above this is the d parameter of a suspension To remedy this we lowered the center of mass on M and lowered the blades on M to ensure that the pickup point of m is above the center of mass and the blade tips leading to M are below the center of mass Initially we were worried that the suspension was still drifting but after a few days and relieving some rubbing the pitch drift was gone Currently we lowered the center of mass further to see if our theory on why the pitch drift stopped is correct but the suspension hasn't had enough time to settle yet The blades are currently quite low mm below there nominal values At some point we hope to raise them to a more reasonable height off nominal To help raise the blades and buy both us an Hanford some margin of stability Betsy is getting some parts fabricated to raise the d value of the suspension Attached is a long drift log with a short description of the many configurations and plots of their pitch F F F are the three bosems that contribute to pitch DAMP P INMON should be calibrated to microradians SUS https://alog.ligo-la.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=74155 Jorge Stuart H Stuart A TJ many others both on and off site SHORT VERSION The BBSS used to drift We have found a BBSS configuration that doesn't drift after some extended settling time However the BBSS configuration that doesn't drift has extreme blade positions so we hope to change d and d parameters to get a more "healthy" BBSS We have been fighting a pitch drift in the BBSS for some time Here is what we know The pitch drift is not a thermal effect and is seen always in one direction The daily drift due to temperature can sometimes be seen on top of the pitch drift but the drift dominates The drift is usually pretty linear over long periods of time The drift is primarily in the top mass M and M stages see far less of the drift but do move slowly as the top mass moves Since the drift is dominated by M we have tried a lot of different configurations Initially we thought the blades that hold the wire leading from M to M was to high this is related to the d parameter of a suspension So we lowered the blades and tried a couple different configurations Then it was discovered that the issue was not from the blades on M but rather the point where M is supported The "pickup" point of M was below the center of mass while nominally it should be above this is the d parameter of a suspension To remedy this we lowered the center of mass on M and lowered the blades on M to ensure that the pickup point of m is above the center of mass and the blade tips leading to M are below the center of mass Initially we were worried that the suspension was still drifting but after a few days and relieving some rubbing the pitch drift was gone Currently we lowered the center of mass further to see if our theory on why the pitch drift stopped is correct but the suspension hasn't had enough time to settle yet The blades are currently quite low mm below there nominal values At some point we hope to raise them to a more reasonable height off nominal To help raise the blades and buy both us an Hanford some margin of stability Betsy is getting some parts fabricated to raise the d value of the suspension Attached is a long drift log with a short description of the many configurations and plots of their pitch F F F are the three bosems that contribute to pitch DAMP P INMON should be calibrated to microradians SUS This is a good question which doesn't yet have a final answer at this time Traditionally such glitches have been called "Low Frequency Burst" and the Machine Learning part of Gravity Spy has applied this label to the present subject But if we look at it closely we can see that it must have been caused by scattered light The bright feature around time seconds is the top of one arch with a faint parallel arch above it culminating near Hz and a second faint arch culminating near time seconds is visible in the fourth frame Looking not just at this one subject but at many hundreds of subjects it is part of a large population of glitches tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk that form a continuum between such low frequency examples and examples with rows of obvious bright arches culminating around Hz So you have a choice here Personally I've been classifying similar subjects as Scattered Light but others might disagree The low frequency examples have less impact on gravitational wave detections than examples rising to higher frequencies so it might make sense to maintain a distinction between them even though the same glitch cause it at work Nowadays we no longer get the splendid wide multi arch forms of Scattered Light that are illustrated in the Field Guide Those were fixed in January before the end of the third observing run By the way It's "Livingston" no "e" and "O4" big Oh four rather than zero four indicating the fourth Advanced LIGO observing run I've adjusted the discussion title accordingly Unfortunately a capital letter O and a digit look very similar in Zooniverse Talk https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3518340/ Marie Celeste I can never remember what this is 28Hz https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3518396/ 90Hz Scattered light https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3518406/ Nice one! available as a glitch class in the level and workflows in levels they can be classified as None Of The Above Likewise for other kinds of glitches when they show up in a workflow that doesn't yet have a suitable class for them Hashtags are optional They work well in smaller projects where there's a prescribed list of them and where everyone adheres to the same discipline They work less well with our huge number of subjects and with new sorts of glitches turning up every month during observing runs Moreover hashtags are prone to being mis spelt and they are liable to get used in questions and discussions where they don't actually apply to the subject at hand Collections of subjects are more robust and more versatile They can be referenced as a whole and specially curated collections could even serve as training sets for the Gravity Spy Machine Learning To start a collection or to add the current subject to a collection click on the button that looks like an itemized list between the      I changed the flow of the TCSY chiller from 0gpm to 7gpm These Thermoflex chillers have their flow rate adjusted by opening or closing a way valve at the back of the chiller for both X and Y chillers these have been in the full open position with the lever pointed straight up The Y chiller has been running with 0gpm so our only change was a lower flow rate The X chiller has been at 7gpm already and the manual states that these chillers shouldn't be ran below 8gpm Though this was a small note in the manual and could be easily missed Since the flow couldn't be increased via the way valve on back I didn't want to lower it further and left it as is Two questions came from this Why are we running so close to the 8gpm minimum? Why is the flow rate for the X chiller so low? The flow rate has been consistent for the last year so I don't suspect that the pumps are getting worn out As far back as I can trend they have been around and with some brief periods above or below commissioning period we made several adjustments to the settings of the TCS ring heater These changes aimed to investigate whether we could reduce the amplitude of a peak around Hz observed in DARM which we suspect may be associated with input jitter noise coupling into DARM At approximately UTC we began by reducing the ring heater RH power per segment on ITMY from W to W After one hour around UTC we increased the power on the ETMX ring heaters per segment from W to W Finally at about UTC we changed the TCS setting of the ETMY RH per segment from W to W While adjusting the RH settings we monitored the effects on various parameters including sideband power buildup in the PRC the interferometer reflectivity and the optical gain We would expect these values to be stable if all variables remained constant Here are some notable observations The optical gain increased by approximately following the RH changes The PRC power buildups at MHz and MHz decreased by approximately to There may have been a slight improvement in optical gain of less than The power in the Power Recycling Cavity POP A LF and the interferometer reflected power REFL A LF increased although the effect was minimal for both signals Power at the AS port as measured by the AS C QPD showed a decrease with actual counts dropping about to representing a reduction of around Overall the changes in the different signals observed in the first plot were relatively small across most buildups with the optical gain showing a slight increase or remaining stable during the RH setting changes for ITMY ETMX and ETMY In the second attachment we present the DARM data between and Hz along with the changes in the height of the hump around Hz following each adjustment to the relative humidity RH settings It appears that the most significant effect on the amplitude of the Hz hump occurred after the reduction of the ETMY RH power indicated by the blue trace This effect was more pronounced compared to the changes observed hour after the IY RH adjustment green and hour after the EX RH adjustment orange brown In the third attachment we present the DARM jitter coherence The power spectra for the DARM and IMC WFS A are shown in the second and third plots because they serve as the best indicators for measuring input jitter The first plot displays the coherence between IMC WFS A and DARM as well as the coherence between PEM PSL PERISCOPE and DARM We observe approximately coherence between the IMC WFS A I PIT and the PEM PSL PERISCOPE X with DARM and around coherence between the IMC WFS A I YAW and DARM In conclusion it is uncertain whether the last change had any significant impact but maintaining these RH settings seemed safe Overall we did not make the situation worse so we saved these RH values in script There had been some issues with processing the In Lock SUS Charge Measurements for this past week so I looked at the script and was able to fix the issue Originally the way that the script would figure out whether it needs to run a measurement or whether it had already been processed is that it would make a list of all the measurements that occurred during the entered time period default is the past month and a list of all processed measurements that occurred during the entered time period and then uses nested for loops to check whether a processed file existed for each data file That normally works fine but in this case the last time we had gotten and processed measurements was over one month ago so when the script tried making a list of the processed files from within the last month there weren't any and the list was blank Then when it tried to iterate over each data file and then over each processed file it would skip the entire processed file iteration because the list was empty The range over which it looks for unprocessed files can be changed or set to look at all files in each directory but that shouldn't be required in this most cases so I edited the script I added in a catch for when the coefficient file list is empty for it to run all measurements in the data directory list This update works and has been committed to svn I'd call this a "Yes" but this relies on what's explained in the Tutorial for the GS level workflow Note that the arches in the strain channel and in the auxiliary channel are accurately aligned in time culminating at the same moments What's going on here is that some laser light is scattered into the vicinity of the X end test mass ETMX reflected by the gold plated electrostatic traces on the reaction mass RM behind ETMX see here tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk for a lot of pictures reflected by the rear side of the reflective mirror coating on the front face of ETMX reflected again by the RM electrodes and a few times more and on each back and forth trip a little stray light at the wrong phase leaks back through the highly reflective coating to rejoin the circulating light in the X arm When the reaction mass is moving by a few relative to the test mass the phase relationships change and these changes are what's showing up as noise The channel L ASC X TR A NSUM OUT DQ measures the total amount of laser light making it through the ETMX coating to reach the transmission monitoring tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3045700?comment system behind the reaction mass It is mostly sensitive at very low frequencies so it sees the low frequency part of the Scattered Light glitches coming from light that has been reflected only once at the RM In the strain channel everything below Hz is buried under stationary background noise suppressed in the image but above Hz it is much more sensitive than the auxiliary channel so it "sees" the upper arches coming from multiple reflections between ETMX and RM The Field Guide entry for "Scattered Light" links to a relevant paper The Gravity Spy workflows are still somewhat experimental various subject sets of
