https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3530880/ "Same folks" is quite broad there are probably tens of thousands of people involved overall ! On the one hand there's the large international community of astrophysicists whether affiliated with institutes that are part of the LIGO Virgo KAGRA collaboration or members of other institutions working with already published raw data from the earlier observing runs Then there are the theoretical astrophysicists who run vast numerical simulations and to whom we owe the precomputed waveform templates against which the measured strain signal is compared in real time by several of the science data pipelines And then there are the many many people keeping things running and already preparing for the next round of upgrades! on the engineering side Operators and vacuum technicians and electrical engineers and facilities staff on site commissioners and detector characterization DetChar specialists for tuning calibration and noise hunting the teams at the LIGO labs at CalTech and MIT the teams at cooperating institutions responsible for specific hardware components and also the commercial suppliers of all the off the shelf and custom bits and pieces Yes chirp waveforms from binary black hole mergers can be and have been turned into sound waves Doing it well is tricky the events happen in a fraction of a second and most of their content is at rather low frequencies so if you just play the waveform as is you'll hear a quick dull "clonk" rather than a bird like "chirp" Play it faster and it'll rise to higher frequencies but it'll be over even more quickly Slow it down to last longer and it'll go below human hearing range Reprocess it to last longer and happen at higher frequencies and it's nice to listen to but the original waveform will have been modified beyond recognition and will no longer be of astrophysical use Some people at Virgo involved in educational outreach have even used a grand piano to imitate the waveforms reading a spectrogram as if it was a musical score The software producing our Q transform spectrograms which is also called "Gravity Spy" tries to adapt to the glitch at hand using fine time resolution with coarse frequency resolution low Q for short duration broadband things like Blips fine frequency resolution and coarse time resolution high Q in the opposite case g for longer duration noise at a nearly constant frequency and in between settings for in between cases whichever choice results in an image with the highest contrast This works well in many cases but sometimes the choice turns out to be sub optimal and sometimes it picks entirely the wrong setting One and the same glitch can look very different tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk depending on how it has been processed https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3530578/ Worth a try but if it that complicated I Background noise is inevitable in this undertaking the variations in the photodiode current at the detection end of the interferometers are still up to a million times larger than the signal we want to measure and a lot of noise suppression and noise subtraction and calibration are applied before the science pipelines get to see the bit stream that represents the measured spacetime distortion gravitational strain Even more effort has gone into keeping most of the noise from reaching the photodiodes in the first place Our subject images partly for historical reasons are created from data that have been partially but not completely cleaned and the Gravity Spy software applies its own less sophisticated whitening on minute long chunks of data which makes the background behind the transient glitches and occasional chirps look like completely random white noise Without this whitening step every image would be bright yellow towards the Hz bottom edge where there's four orders of magnitude more noise than around Hz and green towards the top edge due to quantum shot noise and crisscrossed by numerous narrow yellow and green horizontal spectral tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk lines The Detector Status Summary Pages tab ! ASD sensitivity curves The low frequency background mainly comes from micro seismic ground motion thermal noise in the test mass reflective coatings and angular sensing and control noise The main contribution at high frequencies is quantum shot noise from individual photon interactions with the detection photodiodes already greatly reduced by using squeezed light Many individual peaks are visible roll modes of the test mass suspensions near Hz a cluster of calibration spectral lines around Hz bounce and roll modes of some optics suspensions near and Hz the Hz mains and its harmonics many small humps from beam jitter starting around Hz the violin modes of the beam splitter suspension at just over Hz Hanford's ADF line now at Hz the violin modes of the test mass suspensions around Hz and multiples You might enjoy a glance at P Nguyen al Environmental Noise in Advanced LIGO Detectors tab reporting the state of affairs by the end of O This and other publications and preprints are linked from our Talk > Help > Resources tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk page https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3530578/ Hanford's beam jitter cleaning has just been re tuned once again LHO tab Spot the difference In particular the hump around Hz has almost disappeared for now Click the image for a full size view ! I'd call this a "Yes" but this relies on what's explained in the Tutorial for the GS level workflow Note that the arches in the strain channel and in the auxiliary channel are accurately aligned in time culminating at the same moments What's going on here is that some laser light is scattered into the vicinity of the X end test mass ETMX reflected by the gold plated electrostatic traces on the reaction mass RM behind ETMX see here tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk for a lot of pictures reflected by the rear side of the reflective mirror coating on the front face of ETMX reflected again by the RM electrodes and a few times more and on each back and forth trip a little stray light at the wrong phase leaks back through the highly reflective coating to rejoin the circulating light in the X arm When the reaction mass is moving by a few relative to the test mass the phase relationships change and these changes are what's showing up as noise The channel L ASC X TR A NSUM OUT DQ measures the total amount of laser light making it through the ETMX coating to reach the transmission monitoring tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 3045700?comment system behind the reaction mass It is mostly sensitive at very low frequencies so it sees the low frequency part of the Scattered Light glitches coming from light that has been reflected only once at the RM In the strain https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3530880/ "Same folks" is quite broad there are probably tens of thousands of people involved overall ! On the one hand there's the large international community of astrophysicists whether affiliated with institutes that are part of the LIGO Virgo KAGRA collaboration or members of other institutions working with already published raw data from the earlier observing runs Then there are the theoretical astrophysicists who run vast numerical simulations and to whom we owe the precomputed waveform templates against which the measured strain signal is compared in real time by several of the science data pipelines And then there are the many many people keeping things running and already preparing for the next round of upgrades! on the engineering side Operators and vacuum technicians and electrical engineers and facilities staff on site commissioners and detector characterization DetChar specialists for tuning calibration and noise hunting the teams at the LIGO labs at CalTech and MIT the teams at cooperating institutions responsible for specific hardware components and also the commercial suppliers of all the off the shelf and custom bits and pieces Yes chirp waveforms from binary black hole mergers can be and have been turned into sound waves Doing it well is tricky the events happen in a fraction of a second and most of their content is at rather low frequencies so if you just play the waveform as is you'll hear a quick dull "clonk" rather than a bird like "chirp" Play it faster and it'll rise to higher frequencies but it'll be over even more quickly Slow it down to last longer and it'll go below human hearing range Reprocess it to last longer and happen at higher frequencies and it's nice to listen to but the original waveform will have been modified beyond recognition and will no longer be of astrophysical use Some people at Virgo involved in educational outreach have even used a grand piano to imitate the waveforms reading a spectrogram as if it was a musical score The software producing our Q transform spectrograms which is also called "Gravity Spy" tries to adapt to the glitch at hand using fine time resolution with coarse frequency resolution low Q for short duration broadband things like Blips fine frequency resolution and coarse time resolution high Q in the opposite case g for longer duration noise at a nearly constant frequency and in between settings for in between cases whichever choice results in an image with the highest contrast This works well in many cases but sometimes the choice turns out to be sub optimal and sometimes it picks entirely the wrong setting One and the same glitch can look very different Background noise is inevitable in this undertaking the variations in the photodiode current at the detection end of the interferometers are still up to a million times larger than the signal we want to measure and a lot of noise suppression and noise subtraction and calibration are applied before the science pipelines get to see the bit stream that represents the measured spacetime distortion gravitational strain Even more effort has gone into keeping most of the noise from reaching the photodiodes in the first place Our subject images partly for historical reasons are created from data that have been partially but not completely cleaned and the Gravity Spy software applies its own less sophisticated whitening on minute long chunks of data which makes the background behind the transient glitches and occasional chirps look like completely random white noise Without this whitening step every image would be bright yellow towards the Hz bottom edge where there's four orders of magnitude more noise than around Hz and green towards the top edge due to quantum shot noise and crisscrossed by numerous narrow yellow and green horizontal spectral tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk lines The Detector Status Summary Pages tab ! ASD sensitivity curves The low frequency background mainly comes from micro seismic ground motion thermal noise in the test mass reflective coatings and angular sensing and control noise The main contribution at high frequencies is quantum shot noise from individual photon interactions with the detection photodiodes already greatly reduced by using squeezed light Many individual peaks are visible roll modes of the test mass suspensions near Hz a cluster of calibration spectral lines around Hz bounce and roll modes of some optics suspensions near and Hz the Hz mains and its harmonics many small humps from beam jitter starting around Hz the violin modes of the beam splitter suspension at just over Hz Hanford's ADF line now at Hz the violin modes of the test mass suspensions around Hz and multiples You might enjoy a glance at P Nguyen al Environmental Noise in Advanced LIGO Detectors tab reporting the state of affairs by the end of O This and other publications and preprints are linked from our Talk > Help > Resources tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk page https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3530578/ Hanford's beam jitter cleaning has just been re tuned once again LHO tab Spot the difference In particular the hump around Hz has almost disappeared for now Click the image for a full size view ! I'll try to be brief and summarize it from a bird's eye point of view For further details I recommend The LIGO Scientific Collaboration the Virgo Collaboration B P Abbott al A guide to LIGO Virgo detector noise and extraction of transient gravitational wave signals tab D Davis al LIGO Detector Characterization in the Second and Third Observing Runs tab and for one egregious special case the one that had given rise to the Gravity Spy logo image C Pankow al Mitigation of the instrumental noise transient in gravitational wave data surrounding GW tab Note first that glitches our main concern in this Zooniverse project are just a minor side show in the big picture If you took a hundred thousand Gravity Spy subjects spanning seconds each assume no overlaps and put them side by side they would cover less than days' worth of observing time Most of the observing time is free of glitches loud enough to produce Gravity Spy subjects The data cleaning performed in real time and repeated more slowly and more carefully after the end of an observing run whilst preparing the next issue of the GW event catalogue publication is mostly concerned with stationary noise contributions to the recorded data stream that are of instrumental or terrestrial origin and that are always present or present on timescales much longer than a few seconds The major ideas are Keep sources of noise away from the test masses from the auxiliary optics and from the detection photodiodes Seismic isolation suspensions active feedforward cancellation of remaining seismic effects somewhat similar to how noise cancelling headphones work Apply narrow notch filters g to remove the higher mains harmonics at multiples of Hz the violin modes of the test mass suspensions and the calibration lines that are intentionally injected Subtract contributions that can be accurately predicted from measurements of auxiliary channels E the effects via magnetic fields at the Hz mains frequency are measured by dozens of voltage sensors current sensors and magnetometers Their coupling to the strain channel is periodically measured by using large coils to inject magnetic field noise broadband or at specific frequencies and measuring its effects both in the magnetometers and in the strain channel from which the transfer function from each magnetometer channel to the strain channel can be computed which can subsequently used for noise subtraction Likewise for mechanical noises sensed by geophones accelerometers and microphones shakers and large loudspeakers are used for injections here Calibrate the result by moving the test masses by known tiny amounts and measuring the effect in the strain channel Moving the test masses for this purpose is mainly performed by light pressure auxiliary lasers "Photon calibrators" operating at a mere couple of watts modulated under computer control at several frequencies A completely independent method rarely used at LIGO but regularly at Virgo are Newtonian calibrators a wheel with two heavy tungsten masses is set to rotate very carefully balanced and vibration isolated outside the vacuum chambers but close to one test mass Its gravitational attraction of the test mass is very slightly larger when the tungsten blocks are in line with the test mass than when they are at right angles This is a purely non relativistic near field effect unrelated to gravitational waves It decreases with the fourth power of distance between the wheel and the test mass In addition a few more calibration lines at low frequencies around Hz are injected through the test mass suspensions The filtering the noise subtraction and the application of the current calibration factors all happen in software on dedicated real time computers for the path that feeds the real time science pipelines A side branch turns off before the line subtraction to feed the near real time glitch detection software "Omicron" and the software that turns Omicron triggers into Gravity Spy images The diagram you cite shows a modest analog hardware setup used temporarily for measuring the violin modes of one test mass suspension after a test mass had been replaced and suspended on a new quartet of fused silica fibers The new resonances need to be determined with milliHertz accuracy in order to filter them out later and to actively damp them when they get rung up finest frequency resolution at the expense of coarsest time resolution They become easier to recognize once you've looked at hundreds or thousands of them and seen more of the extent of the whole I'll try to be brief and summarize it from a bird's eye point of view For further details I recommend The LIGO Scientific Collaboration the Virgo Collaboration B P Abbott al A guide to LIGO Virgo detector noise and extraction of transient gravitational wave signals tab D Davis al LIGO Detector Characterization in the Second and Third Observing Runs tab and for one egregious special case the one that had given rise to the Gravity Spy logo image C Pankow al Mitigation of the instrumental noise transient in gravitational wave data surrounding GW tab Note first that glitches our main concern in this Zooniverse project are just a minor side show in the big picture If you took a hundred thousand Gravity Spy subjects spanning seconds each assume no overlaps and put them side by side they would cover less than days' worth of observing time Most of the observing time is free of glitches loud enough to produce Gravity Spy subjects The data cleaning performed in real time and repeated more slowly and more carefully after the end of an observing run whilst preparing the next issue of the GW event catalogue publication is mostly concerned with stationary noise contributions to the recorded data stream that are of instrumental or terrestrial origin and that are always present or present on timescales much longer than a few seconds The major ideas are Keep sources of noise away from the test masses from the auxiliary optics and from the detection photodiodes Seismic isolation suspensions active feedforward cancellation of remaining seismic effects somewhat similar to how noise cancelling headphones work Apply narrow notch filters g to remove the higher mains harmonics at multiples of Hz the violin modes of the test mass suspensions and the calibration lines that are intentionally injected Subtract contributions that can be accurately predicted from measurements of auxiliary channels E the effects via magnetic fields at the Hz mains frequency are measured by dozens of voltage sensors current sensors and magnetometers Their coupling to the strain channel is periodically measured by using large coils to inject magnetic field noise broadband or at specific frequencies and measuring its effects both in the magnetometers and in the strain channel from which the transfer function from each magnetometer channel to the strain channel can be computed which can subsequently used for noise subtraction Likewise for mechanical noises sensed by geophones accelerometers and microphones shakers and large loudspeakers are used for injections here Calibrate the result by moving the test masses by known tiny amounts and measuring the effect in the strain channel Moving the test masses for this purpose is mainly performed by light pressure auxiliary lasers "Photon calibrators" operating at a mere couple of watts modulated under computer control at several frequencies A completely independent method rarely used at LIGO but regularly at Virgo are Newtonian calibrators a wheel with two heavy tungsten masses is set to rotate very carefully balanced and vibration isolated outside the vacuum chambers but close to one test mass Its gravitational attraction of the test mass is very slightly larger when the tungsten blocks are in line with the test mass than when they are at right angles This is a purely non relativistic near field effect unrelated to gravitational waves It decreases with the fourth power of distance between the wheel and the test mass In addition a few more calibration lines at low frequencies around Hz are injected through the test mass suspensions The filtering the noise subtraction and the application of the current calibration factors all happen in software on dedicated real time computers for the path that feeds the real time science pipelines A side branch turns off before the line subtraction to feed the near real time glitch detection software "Omicron" and the software that turns Omicron triggers into Gravity Spy images The diagram you cite shows a modest analog hardware setup used temporarily for measuring the violin modes of one test mass suspension after a test mass had been replaced and suspended on a new quartet of fused silica fibers The new resonances need to be determined with milliHertz accuracy in order to filter them out later and to actively damp them when they get rung up I would answer "Yes" here the auxiliary channel coming from the small fraction of laser light that makes it through the highly reflective mirror coating on Hanford's X end test mass which is sensed in order to monitor and control the proper beam alignment does witness the extremely loud glitch in the main gravitational strain channel This is mentioned in the Tutorial for the Gravity Spy level workflow Different channels can have very different sensitivities to noise at lower or higher frequencies The H ASC X TR A PIT OUT DQ channel is more sensitive towards very low frequencies even below the Hz bottom edge of the image and less sensitive above Hz The strain channel is less sensitive below Hz and more sensitive at frequencies of a few hundred Hz Therefore the resulting glitch shapes are quite different but they coincide quite accurately on the time axis and both channels show a taller shape followed by a less tall one compairson to models started in Apoloiges for the large numer of plots The main message is that we have a decent model of the quantum noise from October see this and this plot can get a fairly independent constraint on homodyne angle and SRC detunings from these squeezer data sets without the filter cavity and some loose estimates for arm power based on squeezer losses There is a discrepancy between the model and the data in the traces taken near anti squeezing without the filter cavity that is interesting and I haven't tried to model mode mismatches yet Outline of how this model is made start with an assumption about arm power 365kW Later we can check how this model changes with arm power changed use noise budget estimate of technical noise at kHz measured ASD and assumption about arm power to fit IFO readout efficenecy here compare to known readout losses from google sheet expected from OFI pass OM OM OMC QPD pick off OMC throughput DCPD QE This implies unknown readout losses including IFO to OMC mode mismatch but this depends on the arm power we start with use the best sqz and anti sqz either with or without filter cavity subtracting noise budget estimate of technical noise at kHz to estimate total squeezer efficiency and nonlinear gain Set the squeezer injection losses so that the total squeezer efficiency is injection losses IFO readout losses This gives us injection losses compared to known injection losses from the google sheet for OPO SFI passes FC WFS pick off ZMs OFI sqz injection and SRC losses this gives us unknown injection losses A mode mismatch could cause a different readout loss for the IFO beam than for the squeezer so this assingment of losses could be incorrect if there is a large mode mismatch between the IFO and the OMC The code fits the squeezing angle for anti squeezing and squeezing traces to either maximize or minimize quantum noise For the other squeezing angles mid squeezing from sqz or a sqz it uses a fit This fit starts with an estimate of the non quantum noise made by subtracting the measure DARM asd without squeezing from the quantum noise model without squeezing from Hz to 2300Hz and adds that to a quantum noise model to fit the squeezing angle The procedure up to this point should force all the models to match the measurements at 2kHz but not at mid or low frequencies The first two attachments show data from mid October separated into two different plots one with mid squeezing one with degrees from sqz and a sqz to make it easier to read We can look at the mid and low frequencies to help us constrain the model for homodyne angle SRC detuning and maybe mode matching and FC parameters With the filter cavity the traces that are degrees from squeezing and anti squeezing don't provide much information we can probably skip these in future data sets but the ones degrees from anti squeezing without the filter cavity are interesting Arm power We can get some constraints on arm power by assuming that all of our unknown loss is injection loss or all readout loss this gives us a range of 327kW 381kW with a homodyne angle of degrees and no SRC detuning Attached are plots made for the high and lower power models by clicking back and forth you can see that the lowest powers seem to disagree with the low frequency data implying that some of our unknown losses truly are readout losses but this isn't a very precise way to estimate arm power SRC detuning Without the filter cavity the mid squeezing traces are most clearly sensitive to SRC detuning shown in this attachment where the SRC detuning of degrees is clearly too large You can flip through these SRC plots which suggests that our SRC detuning at the time of these measurements was between and degrees I'll leave it at degrees or 1mrad in the model Homodyne angle In we noticed that anti squeezing without the filter cavity is very sensitive to the homodyne angle and that we've been using the wrong sign for our modeling in O Here are plots that reaffirm that the negative homodyne angle is wrong with mid squeezing as we did in and with squeezing angle 10degrees from squeezing and anti squeezing which also clearly shows the problem for those traces near anti squeezing It's also nice to notice that the mid sqz traces aren't especially sensitive to homodyne angle in the mid frequency range taht we were using to set the SRC detuning so this data set without the filter cavity can give us fairly independent constraints on SRC detuning and homodyne angle Here is a plot of the homodyne angle of degrees based on without the squeezing traces so that it's easier to see what's happening There is a large discrepancy between the model and FDAS degrees from 55Hz and there is also a smaller discrepancy for FDAS degrees in this frequency range This discrepancy can be redcued a bit by making the homodyne angle larger but that doesn't seem to be a good model of the data so this discrepancy is probably due to something we aren't modeling correctly here Filter cavity detuning We have used 33Hz as the filter cavity detuning but data from mid squeezing with the filter cavity suggests that the OMC The code fits the squeezing angle for anti squeezing and squeezing traces to either maximize or minimize quantum noise For the other squeezing angles mid squeezing from sqz or a sqz it uses a fit This fit starts with an estimate of the non quantum noise made by subtracting the measure DARM asd without squeezing from the quantum noise model without squeezing from Hz to 2300Hz and adds that to a quantum noise model to fit the squeezing angle The procedure up to this point should force all the models to match the measurements at 2kHz but not at mid or low frequencies The first two attachments show data from mid October separated into two different plots one with mid squeezing one with degrees from sqz and a sqz to make it easier to read We can look at the mid and low frequencies to help us constrain the model for homodyne angle SRC detuning and maybe mode matching and FC parameters With the filter cavity the traces that are degrees from squeezing and anti squeezing don't provide much information we can probably skip these in future data sets but the ones degrees from anti squeezing without the filter cavity are interesting Arm power We can get some constraints on arm power by assuming that all of our unknown loss is injection loss or all readout loss this gives us a range of 327kW 381kW with a homodyne angle of degrees and no SRC detuning Attached are plots made for the high and lower power models by clicking back and forth you can see that the lowest powers seem to disagree with the low frequency data implying that some of our unknown losses truly are readout losses but this isn't a very precise way to estimate arm power SRC detuning Without the filter cavity the mid squeezing traces are most clearly sensitive to SRC detuning shown in this attachment where the SRC detuning of degrees is clearly too large You can flip through these SRC plots which suggests that our SRC detuning at the time of these measurements was between and degrees I'll leave it at degrees or 1mrad in the model Homodyne angle In we noticed that anti squeezing without the filter cavity is very sensitive to the homodyne angle and that we've been using the wrong sign for our modeling in O Here are plots that reaffirm that the negative homodyne angle is wrong with mid squeezing as we did in and with squeezing angle 10degrees from squeezing and anti squeezing which also clearly shows the problem for those traces near anti squeezing It's also nice to notice that the mid sqz traces aren't especially sensitive to homodyne angle in the mid frequency range taht we were using to set the SRC detuning so this data set without the filter cavity can give us fairly independent constraints on SRC detuning and homodyne angle Here is a plot of the homodyne angle of degrees based on without the squeezing traces so that it's easier to see what's happening There is a large discrepancy between the model and FDAS degrees from 55Hz and there is also a smaller discrepancy for FDAS degrees in this frequency range This discrepancy can be redcued a bit by making the homodyne angle larger but that doesn't seem to be a good model of the data so this discrepancy is probably due to something we aren't modeling correctly here Filter cavity detuning We have used 33Hz as the filter cavity detuning but data from mid squeezing with the filter cavity suggests that the detuning in this data set closer to Hz Here is a series of plots to show how mid sqz is sensitive to FC detuning The last two plots are with the final model paramters it is a reasonably good description of the data with the main discrepancy remaining in the anti squeezing without the filter cavity The scripts parameters and data used to make these plots is in quantumnoisebudgeting commit https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=82140 D Davis E Capote O Patane There was a discussion recently in the Detchar tools channel about how to interpret the cumulative range plots generated on the summary pages such as today's cumulative range plot Specifically it seems incorrect that we could accumulate of our range below Hz Derek has pointed out that this is so misleading because the calculation of cumulative range in this manner is actually performed somewhat incorrectly In short range can be thought as analogous to SNR which is a quantity that must be added in quadrature Therefore the order matters when calculating a cumulative range e the range acquired from Hz then Hz Hz etc Therefore the total cumulative range number as in the one we think about all the time Mpc for example is correct but determining the range over a subset of the band such as Hz needs to be done more carefully so it is not misleading Once we started discussing this I pointed out that this means that the way we compare ranges is also misleading as in when we run our DARM integral comparison scripts we are subtracting the cumulative range of two different DARM PSDs but we subtract it in amplitude Mpc and not in quadrature Mpc Derek has created an improved way to calculate cumulative range which they have coined to be the "cumulative normalized range" To get right to the point it is better to normalize the cumulative range squared by the total range This is an example plot showing how these two differ This plot shows that for a given DARM PSD the cumulative normalized range better estimates the sensitivity gained over a particular range of frequency The low frequency portion is still very important this results from the dependence in the range calculation but indeed we gain very little sensitivity between Hz for example You can also see that when using the normalized method the curve where you integrate up in frequency and the curve where you integrate down in frequency intersect at about of the range which is what you would expect In equation form this image attachment defines the total cumulative range and this image attachment shows our defintion of the normalized cumulative range In order to more sensibly compare two sensitivities by frequency we have also derived a way to calculate the cumulative normalized range difference The derivation is slightly more complicated but the result is that you subtract the two cumulative normalized quantities and then normalize by the sum of the two ranges This image attachment shows the equation form of this To make sense of why this method is better than the method we use now you can imagine that we have two PSDs one with Mpc of range and one that is exactly the same except that between Hz there is an additional gain of Mpc such that the total range is now Mpc If you compare these two bizarre PSDs you would expect that the cumulative range difference between the two from Hz is Mpc and then zero thereafter This is an example plot showing how the cumulative range difference would appear using the method where you subtract the two cumulative ranges and then the method where you apply this normalized range method The normalized range calculation behaves as expected while the method that straightforwardly subtracts the two cumulative ranges overshoots the range gain from Hz and then misleadingly indicates the range is decreasing above Hz to make up for it There is a lot of information to grasp here and Derek and I will be posting a document to the DCC soon with a fuller explanation and full derivations Oli has taken the time to implement these new methods in our DARM comparison scripts and they will follow up here with more information about that Non image of thermal coupling of localized regions of the lab temperature to the test masses This was explored a bit previous in these alogs Environmental to test mass thermal lens coupling aLOG Spatial temperature variations in the LVEA aLOG To study this I looked at a hour lock from late Decemeber Over that time the AVTEMP of the LVEA stays within 1C 15F of the average temperature However ZONE around the BSC chambers and ITMs sees a tempreature excursion event from 56hr to 64hr This indicates that test masses may be be heated during this time which could cause transient thermal lenses with opposite sign to the transient change in the temperature and some time delay If we look at the Hartmann sensor data we indeed see negative lenses start to form around 58hrs Some Finesse modeling earlier indicated that the 9MHz PRG will be impacted by this We do see a corresponding change in RF signal strength as indicated here However there is no corresponding change in the range at least nothing significant Finally there is some indication from tracking fluctiations in test mass eigenmodes that the test masses are getting warmer due to increasing eigenmode frequencies The time delay between the lab temperature change and test mass eigenmode change looks to be about hours This is more circumstantial The interplay of time delays here needs to be properly understood TCS The data originally were in a dataframe of two columns. The first column was the "comment" text and the second was the "URL" affiliated with the comment. After each comment has been formatted such that it is followed by its URL.

    Many of the acronyms relate to channels in LIGO sensors or other processes surrounding LIGO.

Y order For posterity I attach a pdf which shows the entire plot series from the code SeiSVN seismic Common SPI Scripts plot spi motivation "The code" is an updated version of that from LHO Really the only updates are to use the modern version of each of the SPI's DOF's noise budget most recently documented in LHO Please revisit LHO if you'd like to understand the estimate of the ISI platforms that has not changed at all as we have not made substantial performance improvements to the HAM HAM ISIs since remember O started in June and is on going today DISCUSSION A brief bit of discussion about the changes in SPI noise budget SPI LONG See first png or page of the pdf plot series The modern modeled SPI longitudinal IFO performance is worse below Hz where the model now includes a real estimate of the frequency noise of its laser source which is now the PSL with frequency noise from LHO rather than what was proposed in the conceptual design phase an independent laser source with free running NPRO frequency noise Hz rtHz Hz For that same reason it's better above Hz and the limit is instead the next noisiest source in the modern design ADC noise SPI PIT YAW See second png and third png or pages and of the pdf plot series The modern modeled SPI Pitch Yaw optical lever performance is split into two curves one for spot size of mm at the "reflector" ISI e the spot size at "ISIJ" which is HAM in this pathfinder instantiation after having diverged over the traverse and measured by "QPDA" and one for spot size of mm at the "transceiver" ISI e the spot size at "ISIK" which is HAM in this pathfinder instantiation after having been refocused to the original transmitted size by the ROC reflector on HAM and measured by "QPDB" on the HAM transceiver The CDD's model did not account for the spot size increase so it was essentially the mm spot size model The changes in mm spot size model from CDD to FDD are an updated whitened ADC noise curve showing an improvement below Hz and the addition of an estimate for the shot noise on the QPD which makes the > Hz performance slightly worse Both the mm and mm modern estimates are limited by ADC noise across the entire frequency band CONCLUSION My interpretation of the plots regardless of these changes to each DOF of the expected SPI performance comparing these against the estimate of the June performance of the HAM HAM ISI system the conclusions from the conceptual design remain we still expect the pathfinder to provide a range of "interesting" YAW to "delightful" PIT LONG amount of improvement to the system more so in some LIGO Virgo BNS range plot And this is in fact a good illustration of Gravity Spy's purposes and how we can be useful to the observatories On the one hand a few weeks into O4a it was decided to lower the False Alarm Rate threshold for issuing automated public alerts even for insignificant candidate detections to allow two false alarms per science pipeline of which there are eight per day so on average we were going to see more than a dozen public alerts most of which would really come from terrestrial causes per day after allowing for planned and unplanned downtimes On the other hand some kinds of glitches are episodic in nature and when they start happening they tend to happen at eye watering rates When something like these present glitches are ongoing at Hanford while Livingston is having one of the usual bouts of Scattered Light arches due to elevated microseism levels the un modeled search pipelines cWB MLy will spuriously trigger on many chance coincidences of glitches between the two sites More than once I became aware of a bad run of glitches first by looking at GraceDB tab While nowadays almost ten years after GW there's no longer any serious doubt that we really can detect gravitational waves from mergers of compact binary objects it is still as true as ever that great care and diligence must be exercised to not be fooled into mistaking terrestrially caused noise for a real event The important risk is not that some real event might get missed it is that some unreal event is mistaken for a real one and ab used to draw invalid astrophysical conclusions The detectors have become more sensitive over the years and thus they are also picking up ever new kinds of glitches despite all the care taken to keep environmental and technical noise away from the test only updates are to use the modern version of each of the SPI's DOF's noise budget most recently documented in LHO Please revisit LHO if you'd like to understand the estimate of the ISI platforms that has not changed at all as we have not made substantial performance improvements to the HAM HAM ISIs since remember O started in June and is on going today DISCUSSION A brief bit of discussion about the changes in SPI noise budget SPI LONG See first png or page of the pdf plot series The modern modeled SPI longitudinal IFO performance is worse below Hz where the model now includes a real estimate of the frequency noise of its laser source which is now the PSL with frequency noise from LHO rather than what was proposed in the conceptual design phase an independent laser source with free running NPRO frequency noise Hz rtHz Hz For that same reason it's better above Hz and the limit is instead the next noisiest source in the modern design ADC noise SPI PIT YAW See second png and third png or pages and of the pdf plot series The modern modeled SPI Pitch Yaw optical lever performance is split into two curves one for spot size of mm at the "reflector" ISI e the spot size at "ISIJ" which is HAM in this pathfinder instantiation after having diverged over the traverse and measured by "QPDA" and one for spot size of mm at the "transceiver" ISI e the spot size at "ISIK" which is HAM in this pathfinder instantiation after having been refocused to the original transmitted size by the ROC reflector on HAM and measured by "QPDB" on the HAM transceiver The CDD's model did not account for the spot size increase so it was essentially the mm spot size model The changes in mm spot size model from CDD to FDD are an updated whitened ADC noise curve showing an improvement below Hz and the addition of an estimate for the shot noise on the QPD which makes the > Hz performance slightly worse Both the mm and mm modern estimates are limited by ADC noise across the entire frequency band CONCLUSION My interpretation of the plots regardless of these changes to each DOF of the expected SPI performance comparing these against the estimate of the June performance of the HAM HAM ISI system the conclusions from the conceptual design remain we still expect the pathfinder to provide a range of "interesting" YAW to "delightful" PIT LONG amount of improvement to the system more so in some Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling https://alog.ligo-wa.caltech.edu/aLOG/index.php?callRep=83472 Dear Oli It may be useful to remember that when Jeff says that the " input to the suspension at its "Suspension Point" motion for a given suspension can be the quadrature sum of many of the ISI's cartesian degrees of freedom" what he means is that if you want to make a Statistical model which you do and if the DOFs are independant which maybe they are and maybe they are not then using the quadruture sum of the ASDs is a reasonable thing to do In fact the SUSpoint in reality and the calculation of the SUSpoint are done with a linear combination NOT a quadrature sum This means that if you grab some data from the cart basis sensors take the ASDs where you lose the phase and add them in quadrature you will NOT get the ASD of the measured suspoint I think this difference is not going to impact any of your calculations but maybe it will help you avoid aggravation if you try to do some double checking Brian O Patane B LantzAfter seeing my post of the current performance of the H1ISIBS in LHO Brian in his LHO comment rightly cautioned Oli to beware the difference between a "statistical" or "incoherent" model of the CART2EUL projection to the suspension point where one takes the ASDs of the CART DOFs which are inherently only containing amplitude information no phase relation between channels multiplies them by the CART2EUL coefficients and takes the quadrature sum to form an ASD model of the euler basis motion vs a "linear combination" or "coherent" model of the CART2EUL project to the suspension point where the time series of each CART DOF are multiplied by the CART2EUL coefficients the time series are then coherently summed where "coherently" summed just means the amplitude AND phase relationship between the channels has been preserved and then an ASD is taken of that to form an ASD model of the euler basis motion He states "if the DOFs are independent which maybe they are and maybe they are not then using the quadruture sum of the ASDs is a reasonable thing to do " and "I think this difference between and not going to impact any of your calculations"I'd not seen a comparison of these two models either at all or in a long time every chamber SUS combination is different and I had the data so I made the comparison I'll discuss the Euler Basis plots in reverse traditional order because they're easiest to understand progressively that way YAW This plot is uninteresting because the BS projection matrix from CART to EUL has only one unity element mapping RZ directly to Yaw However it lets me introduce what I'll be plotting In the upper panel this shows the both models of ASDs and the underlying Cartesian components multiplied by the CART2EUL matrix element As expected here the thick black dashed ASD the coherent sum model is identical to that think magenta dashed ASD the incoherent sum model The lower panel is the ASD ratio of the linear sum divided by the incoherent sum Of course for this DOF the two models are identical so this ASD ratio is identically across the whole frequency band With me so far? Good P PITCH Here because the Beam Splitter suspension is mounted in the center of the ISI BS optical table yaw'd degrees RX and RY map to PITCH via sqrt with the same sign But the RX and RY performance of the ISI BS is slightly different so the ratio between and is interesting Most notably around the HEPI cross beam foot resonance traditionally called the "HEPI Pier resonance" prior to see LHO the broad feature at Hz where the ASD ratio shows that the incoherent sum model under predicts Sus Point displacement by a factor of 35x r the coherent sum model And then at some other feature at Hz the incoherent sum model is over predicting the Sus Point displacement by 25x ROLL OK now flip the sign of the contribution of RY and watch the coherent sum drop fascinating! The contribution of that same Hz feature is now dramatically over predicted by the incoherent sum by a factor of 5x Are these two the inverse of each other? No! I don't show it explicitly but comparing for roll the inverse of what's plotted and for pitch the Hz number is 74x and 52x respectively so markedly different! VERTICAL Now we're getting really interesting for vertical Z is mapped one to one but RX and RY are contributing in opposite sign and with only roughly the same magnitude rad CART2EUL coefficient The incoherent sum is overestimating the vertical displacement by as much as a factor of 5x where the vertical motion is limited by RX and RY between and Hz Wow!I won't look type thru the rest of the plot because the plot describes it best but boy is it more interesting than I thought it would be TRANSVERSE With transverse even though this degree of freedom "doesn't matter" for the beam splitter now we're cooking with contributing Cartesian degrees of freedom and except for RZ they're all contributing at interesting levels Again you reading the plot is more useful than me describing it here but it's quite interesting that the linear sum predicts more motion between Hz and Hz and the incoherent sum predicts more motion overestimates the motion between to Hz LONGITUDINAL Finally the DOF we work the hardest on shows contribution from all Cartesian degrees of freedom A lucky coincidence perhaps but it looks like the models are about the same for most of the frequency region and the incoherent sum is over predicting the displacement between to Hz which is re enforcing Brian's comment WHAT DOES IT ALL MEAN? Brian is again definitely right to call out that the linear sum model is a better model of the displacement of the Sus Point than the incoherent sum But both I and perhaps even he definitely wasn't expecting factors of 2x discrepancy let alone factors of 5x So I think I might make Brian's conclusion from LHO a little stronger the difference between models will impact the calculations of the Bigger Beam Splitter Suspension BBSS performance so for the update to the seismic input motion I'll not just update the performance from the seisBSC estimate to the current real cartesian performance incoherently projected to the Sus Point but instead update it to the current real euler Sus Point performance computed in the front end CSWG ISC SUS Non image files attached to this report H1ISIBS O Patane B LantzAfter seeing my post of the current performance of the H1ISIBS in LHO Brian in his LHO comment rightly cautioned Oli to beware the difference between a "statistical" or "incoherent" model of the CART2EUL projection to the suspension point where one takes the ASDs of the CART DOFs which are inherently only containing amplitude information no phase relation between channels multiplies them by the CART2EUL coefficients and takes the quadrature sum to form an ASD model of the euler basis motion vs a "linear combination" or "coherent" model of the CART2EUL project to the suspension point where the time series of each CART DOF are multiplied by the CART2EUL coefficients the time series are then coherently summed where "coherently" summed just means the amplitude AND phase relationship between the channels has been preserved and then an ASD is taken of that to form an ASD model of the euler basis motion He states "if the DOFs are independent which maybe they are and maybe they are not then using the quadruture sum of the ASDs is a reasonable thing to do " and "I think this difference between and not going to impact any of your calculations"I'd not seen a comparison of these two models either at all or in a long time every chamber SUS combination is different and I had the data so I made the comparison I'll discuss the Euler Basis plots in reverse traditional order because they're easiest to understand progressively that way YAW This plot is uninteresting because the BS projection matrix from CART to EUL has only one unity element mapping RZ directly to Yaw However it lets me introduce what I'll be plotting In the upper panel this shows the both models of ASDs and the underlying Cartesian components multiplied by the CART2EUL matrix element As expected here the thick black dashed ASD the coherent sum model is identical to that think magenta dashed ASD the incoherent sum model The lower panel is the ASD ratio of the linear sum divided by the incoherent sum Of course for this DOF the two models are identical so this ASD ratio is identically across the whole frequency band With me so far? The details of the proposed sensor rejiggling is a bit involved but the basic idea is that the part of the M to M transfer function coming from the mechanical plant should be reciprocal up to the impedances of the ISI I tried to symmetrize the measured plant by changing the gains of the OSEMs then later by including the possibility that the OSEMs might be seeing off axis motion Three figures and three findings below Finding The reciprocity only allows us to find the relative calibrations of the OSEMs so all of the results below are scaled to the units where the scale of the T OSEM is If we want absolute calibrations we will have to use an independent measurement like the ISI >M transfer functions This will be important when we analyze the results below Figure shows the full 6x M >M transfer function matrix between all of the DOFs in the Euler basis of PR The rows represent the output DOF and the columns represent thr input DOF The dashed lines represent the transpose of the transfer function in question for easier comparison The transfer matrix is not reciprocal Finding The diagonal correction relative to T is given by T T T LF RT SD T T T LF RT SD This shows the difference between RT and LF that Brian saw leading to L Y coupling in the ISI to M transfer functions This also shows the difference between T T and T that leads to the V R coupling that Brian posted in the comment above Since we normalized by T the most likely explanation for the discrepancies is that T and RT are both ish low compared to the other sensors Figure shows the 6x M >M transfer function matrix after applying the scaling factors The main difference is in the Length to Yaw and the Vertical to Roll degrees of freedom as mentioned before Note that the rescaling was made only to make the responses more symmetric the decoupling of the dofs a welcome bonus Finding We can go one step further and allow the sensors to be sensitive to other directions In this case the matrix below is mathematically moving the sensors to where the actuators are in an attempt to collocate them as much as possible T T T LF RT SD T T T LF RT SD I haven't yet found a good interpretation for these numbers beyond the idea that they mean the sensors and actuators are not collocated Three reasons come to mind a The flags and the magnets are a bit off from each other and we are able to pick it up the difference The OSEMs are sensing sideways motion of the flag The actuators are pushing or torquing the suspension in other ways than their intended direction The interesting observation comes when observing Figure After we apply this correction to the sensor side of the transfer function we see a dramatic change in the symmetry and the amplitude of the transfer matrix Particularly the Transverse degree of freedom is much less coupled to both Vertical and Longitudinal Similarly the Pitch to Vertical also improves a bit This is to say by trying to make the plant more reciprocal we also end up decoupling the degrees of freedom We can conclude that there's either miscollocation of the sensor actuator parts of the OSEM or more likely that the OSEMs are reading side motions of the flag because we are able to better see the decoupled plant by just assuming this miscalibration I will post more analysis in the Euler basis later Non image files attached to this report PR M TF Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling like this Second An earthquake that's too strong or strong enough and too close would cause the intererometer to drop out of Observing or to lose lock straight away An earthquake that's not strong enough or too far away may well excite the Hz vibrations but without producing glitches loud enough to show up as Gravity Spy subjects Third Distant earthquakes may induce ground motions well above s but that'll be in the main earthquake band to Hz with not much in the Hz band Examples abound if you like me glance at the Summary Pages every day Fourth For distances above km the induced ground motion stays roughly the same when an earthquake magnitude stronger happens ten times farther away This relationship was exploited g in LHO tab Fifth not all seismic events are created equal They happen at different depths and the extent of the ruptures can vary widely As a result the distribution of ground motion over the bands between and Hz will vary even at similar distances Playing around https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959/ ! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling site may be worth hunting down before O What limited evidence we have so far from GS examples suggests it may reside at the X end Proposed Name Hz scattering serpent ID of proposer Date of proposal arches can culminate at up to a little more than Hz and their flanks can sometimes be traced down as far as about Hz Reported peak frequencies range from to Hz Sometimes Omicron had triggered on a flank rather than a culmination and accordingly reported a peak frequency well below that of the culmination Reported durations can exceed seconds but can also be shorter than seconds when Omicron treated a single flank as one glitch SNRs remain below Renderings at Q are rare while the three higher Q values occur equally often The appearance at Q is more angular emphasizing the flanks while at higher Q the tops of the arches tend to dominate Differential diagnosis Unlike Whistles these arches never reach the Hz top edge Renderings at Q where only the tops of the arches are bright can be https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing!
