This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling site may be worth hunting down before O What limited evidence we have so far from GS examples suggests it may reside at the X end Proposed Name Hz scattering serpent ID of proposer Date of proposal In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959/ ! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at like this Second An earthquake that's too strong or strong enough and too close would cause the intererometer to drop out of Observing or to lose lock straight away An earthquake that's not strong enough or too far away may well excite the Hz vibrations but without producing glitches loud enough to show up as Gravity Spy subjects Third Distant earthquakes may induce ground motions well above s but that'll be in the main earthquake band to Hz with not much in the Hz band Examples abound if you like me glance at the Summary Pages every day Fourth For distances above km the induced ground motion stays roughly the same when an earthquake magnitude stronger happens ten times farther away This relationship was exploited g in LHO tab Fifth not all seismic events are created equal They happen at different depths and the extent of the ruptures can vary widely As a result the distribution of ground motion over the bands between and Hz will vary even at similar distances Playing around https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling site may be worth hunting down before O What limited evidence we have so far from GS examples suggests it may reside at the X end Proposed Name Hz scattering serpent ID of proposer Date of proposal Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959/ ! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959/ ! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959/ ! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Firstly There'll be no glitches for us to admire when LHO isn't observing at the time LHO's duty cycle lately has hovered around thus a third of all candidate earthquakes are expected not to show up like this Second An earthquake that's too strong or strong enough and too close would cause the intererometer to drop out of Observing or to lose lock straight away An earthquake that's not strong enough or too far away may well excite the Hz vibrations but without producing glitches loud enough to show up as Gravity Spy subjects Third Distant earthquakes may induce ground motions well above s https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253/ Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332/ https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084/ Something at Hanford is capable of vibrating for more than a minute at Hz and of reflecting stray light and although these fast scattering "sea serpents" aren't very loud and happen only on rare occasions their rising flanks may have been responsible for more spurious GW candidate alerts per unit of glitchy time than any other class during O And they turn out to be less rare than I thought So the coupling site may be worth hunting down before O What limited evidence we have so far from GS examples suggests it may reside at the X end Proposed Name Hz scattering serpent ID of proposer Date of proposal Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! Just curious Glitches like this first turned up in large numbers at Hanford in spring just before the start of the current fourth observing run O Neither our Machine Learning nor we volunteers nor the detector engineers were expecting them The Machine Learning is mistaking them for Fast Scattering what we on Zooniverse used to call "Crown" which had been the most common kind of glitch at Livingston during O but has been fixed since and no longer occurs In fact they are neither Crowns nor Low Frequency Blips but a peculiar form of Scattered Light They arise as beatnote pulses like the beatnotes you hear when you're tuning a guitar and are almost but not quite in tune To some extent they are due to how the data are processed to turn the into our spectrogram images The present subject along with many others has been processed with very fine time resolution at the expense of very coarse frequency resolution low Q value With a different choice high Q value the frequency resolution could have been fine enough to show very closely spaced parallel fragments of arches and then it would have looked more recognizable When they look like this these glitches have got nicknamed " wheatgrass tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk 2959514?comment " See also the thread O Hanford Scattered Light Fast Scattering tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk illustrated with additional examples for contributing! This is a good question It is due to a combination of two things One is that the LIGO observatories are recording more than a thousand auxiliary channels along with the gravitational strain channel where any real detections are going to appear but where also a great many glitches appear These aux channels come from all sorts of measurements seismometers and geophones sensing the ground motion accelerometers measuring vibrations of the concrete floor and of the vacuum chambers microphones picking up any noise at audible frequencies voltage monitors and magnetometers watching for fluctuations in power supplies and the like weather stations indoor thermometers and then a host of channels keeping track of what all the parts of the interferometers are doing the internal seismic isolation ISI platforms the suspensions of the test masses and of the other major optics power and wavelength fluctuations of the main laser various data about the dozens of auxiliary lasers and so on and so forth Sometimes a few auxiliary channels will witness a glitch in the strain channel picking up a side effect of the same cause Most of the time most aux channels will "see" or "hear" nothing This is why the lower images in the Gravity Spy workflow subjects are often dark aside from some random background noise The other thing is that we're dealing with tens of thousands of glitches each of which could be paired with any one of the many auxiliary channels the total number of possible combinations would be astronomical Thus the researchers had to choose a subset of manageable size The current active subject load in the GS level workflow is limited to a few hundred subjects from the first part O4a May January of the ongoing fourth observing run all from Hanford and each of them in thirty combinations with auxiliary channels randomly picked from a subset of about a hundred channels The chosen subjects represent only a few glitch classes and include no glitches of types that only occurred at Livingston and they come from only a handful of different dates thus they also miss many glitches that occurred at Hanford only during a few shorter episodes Extremely Loud glitches are somewhat over represented in this selection Glitches like the present subject occur at random times at an average rate of one every few hours They are the loudest sort of glitch that the interferometers can with luck! survive without losing lock tab projects zooniverse gravity spy talk The present glitch was more than times louder than the background noise It produced a verbal alert the operator in the control room saw not only some red lights blinking on the screens but also heard a loudspeaker announcing a saturation of the X end test mass suspension Some operators have made a habit of mentioning these alerts in their shift reports and indeed you've been lucky four leaf clover and found such a glitch reported as "EX saturation" at " 25" UTC in LHO tab The present S by the way is one of the counterparts to S If when I find another subject pairing this glitch with an obvious witness in its aux channel I'll try to remember to post about it here Please be welcome to watch out for such examples yourself! https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/331/3623332 https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3624084 Something at https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3630253 Alignment sensing glitches Wavefront sensors As noted above the CHARD and DHARD sensing relies on the beatnotes at and MHz between the main carrier laser light and the sidebands at slightly shorter and longer wavelengths created by phase modulating the laser light But this also means that any glitches arising in the radio frequency modulation signals either merely in those used for the demodulation or already in those sent to the modulators will show up as noise in the CHARD and DHARD channels They will also show up in several Length Sensing and Control LSC channels which rely on the sidebands which don't resonate in the long arms as a comparison basis for the carrier light which does The measurement of the arm length difference where we're looking for gravitational waves does not directly use the sidebands but the strain channel receives feedforward corrections from other LSC channels and glitches in these other LSC channels can enter the strain channel through these correction paths Thus the CHARD channels can sometimes be good witnesses of glitches in the strain channel that are caused by RF modulation glitches This happened for example at Livingston on and is briefly mentioned in the weekly Data Quality shift summary LLO tab ! frame to be continued In general when two or more different timestamps are involved and when they span more than seven days hours the timeline does what it claims to do the tool will display the number of subjects found per week with the first week starting at the event time of the earliest subject e not aligned with calendar weeks When there's only a single event time and thus a zero length time interval between "earliest" and "latest" event the software avoids a division by zero by expanding the blue rectangle to span hours centered on the event time Thus the left edge will be hours before the event time and the right edge hours after the event time up to small rounding errors The time axis in this case will be labeled with two digits for the month a hyphen the two digits day of month a blank space and the two digits hour on the hour clock all in UTC Thus for the present subject the left edge of the blue rectangle winds up about an hour and a half before meaning 27T UTC inferring the year from the event date shown by the nfo button the right edge sits about an hour and a half after meaning 27T and the middle of the rectangle is just a tad to the right of halfway betwee and thus just after 27T UTC Hope this helps! When there are several event times all clustered within less than hours example ask for results from ifo H era O similar to the edges of the rectangle will be close to the earliest and latest event time in the result set However there's some funny rounding going on when the time interval is shorter than a minute and when it gets shorter than a few seconds the time axis tick labels become fairly useless https://www.zooniverse.org/projects/zooniverse/gravity-spy/talk/328/3286959 !
